headline: Hong Kong's Cockatoos Find Home in Artificial Nests
meta_description: Conservation project installs camera-equipped nest boxes to help critically endangered yellow-crested cockatoos breed in urban Hong Kong.
summary_short: Biologists in Hong Kong have installed 15 artificial nest boxes to help critically endangered cockatoos find homes after urban development destroyed 60% of natural tree…
body:
When storm damage and aggressive tree pruning stripped Hong Kong of more than 60% of the natural tree hollows that yellow-crested cockatoos depend on for breeding, the city's roughly 200 wild cockatoos faced an urgent crisis. These descendants of escaped or released pets represent a genetically diverse population of a species with fewer than 2,000 individuals remaining in its native range across eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste. To address what biologist Astrid Andersson describes as "a housing crisis for these birds," she partnered with arborist and conservationist Harry Wong to launch HK Cockatoo Watch. Since March 2025, the team has installed 15 nest boxes fitted with internal cameras across public parks and school campuses, including St. Louis School and ISF Academy, adapting Australian prototypes to suit Hong Kong's humid climate.

The project has already shown promising results. Four of the 15 boxes are currently occupied by breeding pairs, and one housed a chick that was rescued from an apartment air-conditioning vent and reunited with its parents. The chick developed into a fully fledged bird under parental care. What makes this work especially meaningful is its reach beyond conservation biology. Local students have become active participants, drawing the birds for orientation booklets and photographing them during school hours—transforming a wildlife crisis into a learning opportunity.

Harry Wong's vision captures something essential about urban conservation: "How can we coexist with them?" By creating these safe spaces and engaging the next generation, the project demonstrates that cities and wildlife need not exist in conflict. Recent genetic testing shows Hong Kong's cockatoos retain high genetic diversity, suggesting that protecting this urban population could become a vital lifeline for restoring wild cockatoo populations in Southeast Asia.
quick_facts: 200 wild cockatoos now live in Hong Kong, descended from escaped pets
15 artificial nest boxes installed since March 2025 across city parks and schools
Storm damage and tree pruning destroyed over 60% of natural tree hollows
Critically endangered species has fewer than 2,000 individuals left in native range
